'''David Mark Hillis''' (born December 21, 1958) is an American [[evolutionary biologist]], and the Alfred W. Roark Centennial Professor of Biology at the [[University of Texas at Austin]]. He is best known for his studies of molecular evolution, phylogeny, and vertebrate systematics. He created the popular [[Tree of life (biology)|Hillis Plot]] depiction of the evolutionary [[tree of life (biology)|tree of life]].

==Early life==

David Hillis was born in [[Copenhagen]], [[Denmark]] in 1958, the son of William Hillis, an [[epidemiologist]], and Aryge Briggs Hillis, a [[biostatistician]]. Hillis lived his early years in [[Denmark]], [[Belgian Congo]], [[India]], and the [[United States]], where he developed his interests in [[biology]] and [[biodiversity]].  He has two sons, Erec and Jonathan.<ref name="Biological Sciences">

==Education and research==

In 1980 Hillis graduated from [[Baylor University]] with a [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] degree in biology, followed in 1983, 1984, and 1985 with [[Master of Science|M.S.]], [[Master of Philosophy|Ph.M.]], and [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] degrees in [[Biological Science]] from the [[University of Kansas]], specializing in [[molecular evolution]] and [[systematics]].<ref name="Biological Sciences"/>
During this time Hillis developed molecular approaches for reconstructing the evolutionary history of organisms, or [[phylogeny]], with a particular emphasis on the relationships of [[amphibians]]. He also made significant contributions to the understanding of hybridization, molecular processes of evolutionary change, and statistical analysis of biological phylogenies. He continued this research as an assistant professor at the [[University of Miami]] from 1985 to 1987, and then moved to the faculty of the [[University of Texas at Austin]] in 1987.

Hillis received a [[Presidential Young Investigator Award]] from the [[National Science Foundation]] that same year, and was named to the Alfred W. Roark Centennial Professorship in Natural Sciences by the University of Texas in 1992.<ref name="Biological Sciences"/>
His co-authored book ''Molecular Systematics''<ref name="Molecular Systematics">
{{cite book
  | last = Hillis
  | first = David M.
  | title = Molecular Systematics
  | publisher = Sinauer Associates
  | year = 1996
  | orig-year = 1990
  | isbn = 0-87893-282-8
  | display-authors=etal}}
</ref>
was instrumental in developing the field of phylogenetic analysis, and he is a co-author of two of the leading college textbooks on biology (''Life: The Science of Biology''
,<ref name="Life">
{{cite book
  | last = Sadava
  | first = David
  | title = Life: The Science of Biology, 9th ed
  | publisher = Sinauer Associates and [[W. H. Freeman]]
  | orig-year = 2008| year = 2011
  | isbn = 978-1-4292-1962-4
  | display-authors=etal}}
</ref> and ''Principles of Life''
<ref name="Principles of Life">
{{cite book
  | last = Hillis
  | first = David M.
  | title = Principles of Life
  | publisher = Sinauer Associates and [[W. H. Freeman]]
  | year = 2010
  | isbn = 978-1-4292-5721-3
  | display-authors=etal}}
</ref>
). Dr. Hillis was the recipient of a [[MacArthur Fellowship]] in 1999. In 2000, Hillis was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], and in 2008, he was elected a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]]. He has served as president of the [[Society for the Study of Evolution]], and President of the Society of Systematic Biologists. At the University of Texas, he has served as Director of the School of Biological Sciences, Director of the Center for Computational Biology and Bioinformatics, Director of the Dean's Scholars Honors Program of the College of Natural Sciences, and as Chair of the Faculty Council. Hillis also owns and operates the Double Helix Ranch, where he raises Texas Longhorn Cattle.<ref name="Hillis">
{{cite web
|url=http://www.zo.utexas.edu/faculty/antisense/
|title=Hillis and Bull Laboratory
|access-date=2009-01-01
}}
</ref>
